The field is a group, so name it with `aria-labelledby` or `aria-label`. Clicking anywhere in the box focuses the nearest part.
The field shows the locale’s clock. `hourCycle` picks 12 or 24 hours, and `granularity` adds seconds or shows the hour alone. All of them submit 24-hour values.
The parts keep the locale’s order, and the arrow keys follow them on screen.
The root is a group. Each part is a spinbutton named by its unit, like “hour”, with its value and range, and an empty part reads as “Empty”. The text between parts is hidden from screen readers.

The value is a 24-hour time like `"14:30"`, the same as a native time input’s, whatever clock the field shows. It stays `null` until every part holds something. Each part is its own small input: type digits and it moves on, or press A or P for the half of the day.

UI SDK adds a little CSS of its own in a cascade layer named `ui-sdk`. Declare that layer at the top of your global stylesheet, above the Tailwind import, so your classes win over it.
`TimeInput` renders its parts on its own. Add `TimeInputSegments` yourself to put an icon or other content beside them.
`createTimeInputController()` sets, clears or focuses the field from anywhere. Focus a part by its unit, like `"minute"`.
`invalid` marks the field for checks of your own, like an end time before the start.
`locale` sets the order, the separators and the names for the half of the day. Without it, the field follows the page’s language once it’s interactive.
